summary: Pupils (ages 10-11) apply unit-fraction division to real contexts, deciding which structure a story has — partition ('3 people share 1/2 lb → how much each?', 1/2 ÷ 3 = 1/6) versus measurement ('how many 1/3-cup servings in 2 cups?', 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6). The core difficulty is reading the STRUCTURE — which quantity is split, which is the dividend, and whether the answer should grow or shrink — not the arithmetic. Guidance centres on modelling each story on a bar/number line before writing the equation, sanity-checking the answer against 'more or fewer than I started with?', and having pupils invent stories for bare expressions so they run the structure both ways.
misconceptions: Picks the wrong operation — multiplies, or divides in the wrong order (2 ÷ 1/3 done as 1/3 ÷ 2)
Reverses dividend and divisor — computes 3 ÷ 1/2 = 6 for '3 share 1/2 lb' instead of 1/2 ÷ 3
Expects the quotient to be smaller in a measurement problem, so distrusts '6 servings' being more than 2
Sets up the numbers but cannot tell which quantity is being split, so the model does not match the story

activities.title: Build the model, then write the equation
steps: Read a word problem, e.g. 'How many 1/3-cup servings of raisins are in 2 cups?'
Decide whether the story is sharing an amount out among groups (partition) or finding how many portions fit inside an amount (measurement).
Choose and build the matching model on a bar or number line: either share one bar among N people, or fill a 2-cup bar with 1/3-cup portions and count them.
Write the matching division equation (2 ÷ 1/3 = 6) once the picture matches the words.
Lay the story, the picture, and the equation side by side so the three represent the same situation.

If a digital modeller is available, dragging the story onto a bar so the equation and answer recompute live lets pupils see a mismatched picture when they pick the wrong structure — this is one helpful interaction, not a required one.
activities.insight: The story tells you which division it is: sharing an amount out among more than one group gives each less than the whole, while asking how many sub-one-unit portions fit inside an amount gives more than you started with — and the picture either matches the words or it visibly does not.

activities.title: Sort the two structures, name the dividend, then compute
steps: Take several word problems and classify each as 'sharing an amount out' (partition: shared among more than one group, each share is smaller than the amount) or 'how many portions fit' (measurement: when the portion is smaller than one unit, as in these problems, the count is larger than the amount).
Name, for each, which quantity is being split and which is the dividend.
For the sharing problem '3 friends share 1/2 lb of chocolate equally', identify that the half pound is what is cut up, so it is 1/2 ÷ 3, not 3 ÷ 1/2.
After classifying and naming, build the matching bar model and only then write and solve the equation.
activities.insight: Naming the structure and the dividend first helps prevent reversing dividend and divisor and reaching for multiplication out of habit; classifying is a start, but the setup is not complete until the model and equation match the words.

activities.title: Confront 'the answer must get smaller'
steps: Predict, before computing, whether 'how many 1/3-cup servings in 2 cups' should be more or fewer than 2.
Fit 1/3-cup portions into 2 cups on a bar or number line (or with real measuring cups) and count them: there are 6.
State in words why counting portions smaller than one unit inside a larger amount gives a count bigger than the amount.
Contrast: if servings were 3-cup servings instead of 1/3-cup, would there be more or fewer in 2 cups, and why?
activities.insight: A quotient can be larger than the dividend: when you count how many portions smaller than one unit fit inside an amount, the count exceeds the amount.

activities.title: Invent a story for a bare expression, then check it
steps: Write your own word problem that 4 ÷ 1/5 would solve, e.g. 'How many 1/5-metre ribbons can I cut from a 4-metre roll?' (= 20).
Identify which structure your story uses (here, measurement — how many 1/5-sized portions fit in 4).
Solve your own story to confirm it really gives 20 and really matches division, not multiplication.
Check a given answer with the inverse operation, writing e.g. 6 × 1/3 = 2 under the answer to confirm 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6.
activities.insight: Running the structure backwards — building a valid story from the symbols and verifying by the inverse — shows the structure is owned, not merely recognised.

activities.title: Talk through the direction with a context character
steps: Take a kitchen or shop scenario where a character (cook, shopkeeper) poses a sharing problem and a portioning problem.
Before computing, predict aloud whether each answer will be more or fewer than the starting amount, and justify.
Explain to the character which quantity is being split and why.
activities.insight: Articulating the predicted direction and the dividend in a concrete context reinforces structure-reading and the 'more or fewer?' sanity check.

checkQuestion: Solve these two, showing your working: (a) 3 friends share half a pound of chocolate equally — how much does each get? (b) How many 1/3-cup servings of raisins are in 2 cups? Then make up your own word problem that 4 ÷ 1/5 would solve.
checkAnswer: (a) 1/2 ÷ 3 = 1/6 lb each. (b) 2 ÷ 1/3 = 6 servings. Story for 4 ÷ 1/5: any 'how many 1/5-sized portions fit in 4' context, e.g. 'how many 1/5-metre ribbons can I cut from a 4-metre roll?' (= 20).
